Aldous Quill.narrative: I am the tally keeper, and the ledger is the true history of Cullet: every drop that goes in or out of the Store, every debt written, every loss at counters that someone cannot pay. I keep the book open nine to three, and I am the best counters player in town, which is not a boast but a fact Roos Achterberg has learned nightly. My wife Mirren knows everyone's body; I know everyone's debts, and I say less about them than she does. There is one page in the book — the fever winter's — that I hope nobody ever reads closely.
goals: Get the Counting House clock running again, whatever it takes.
Keep the ledger straight and the Store's accounts honest — mostly.
See Sabine settled well, and not with a Strand fisher.
Never be caught out over the fever winter's page.
pastimes: counters under the arcade at night
walking the quay at dusk checking the Store's shutters
reading old ledger pages for pleasure
Aldous Quill.calling: The ledger is my work and my calling: a town that cannot count what it owes is a town that cannot trust itself.
Aldous Quill.mood: watchful and quietly pleased with himself

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She knows more of the town's secrets than I do, and I have never asked her for them.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: Too clever by half, and too taken with old tablets; I want better for her than a fisher's life.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A decent enough lad, but a Strand fisher is not what I raised my daughter for.

relations.name: Lorcan Vane
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: Nine drops owed to the Counting House, and he keeps playing as if the book were a game.

relations.name: Davin Vane
relations.label: debtor's brother
relations.note: A quiet, decent porter; he pays what he can and asks nothing said about it.

relations.name: Anselm Faro
relations.label: lamp keeper
relations.note: The lamp oil is the oldest line in the book; I pay it without question, as my predecessors did.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: counters rival
relations.note: She runs a good game and has never beaten me; I mean to keep it that way.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: reader
relations.note: He keeps the tablets; I keep the book. We understand each other.

relations.name: Petra Tarn
relations.label: creditor
relations.note: The Marver owes her twelve drops; I have written it and will see it settled.

relations.name: Dolly Achterberg
relations.label: debtor
relations.note: She owes Petra Tarn and half the Strand owes her; she keeps her accounts in her head, which I distrust.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: She holds the Cone; I hold the book. We have never needed to quarrel.

relations.name: Kenji Sato
relations.label: ash burner
relations.note: His ash goes into every melt at the Cone, and his figures come to me honest; I wish the rest of the Strand kept accounts as he does.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I wrote the Store's peat out to my own household as paid, twenty drops' worth, and it was never paid.
Davin Vane came to me quietly and paid six drops against Lorcan's debt to the Marver, and asked me to say nothing to his brother. I wrote it.
I beat Roos Achterberg at counters again under the arcade, and she paid her drop with a face like a gull's.
My father showed me the fever winter's page when I was a boy — no, that is wrong; he showed me the oldest pages, the ship-day dues, and told me the clock stopped the day of the Last Sail.
Sabine came home with a tablet rubbing and talked of the Pale till midnight; I told her to mind her lessons and not her fancies.
I paid Anselm Faro for the lamp oil, as the book has every year for eighty-three years, and wondered again who the light is for.

stances.why: A town that cannot count what it owes cannot trust itself.
It is the oldest line in the book; it was paid before me and will be paid after.
Not out of contempt; out of the way the town is built, and the way debts run.
A man who cannot lose a drop gracefully cannot be trusted with a debt.
If the tally keeper's own page is not straight, nothing else can be.

Aldous Quill.secret: In the fever winter the Quills took twenty drops' worth of peat from the Store, and I wrote it in the ledger as paid. It was never paid. Nobody else knows.

Mirren Quill.narrative: I am the only healer and midwife in Cullet, and I have laid out most of the dead on the Crown. I know everyone's body, and most of their secrets come with it. The fever winter taught me that I can nurse a town through a plague and still bury nine of it, and that is a thing I carry every day. Suri Greave is expecting, and I mean to see her safely delivered — and I mean to train a second healer before my hands are too old.
goals: Train a second healer before I am old.
See Suri Greave's child born safely.
Keep my husband's book from being the thing he is remembered for.
Lay the dead out kindly, as I always have.
pastimes: sitting at the wash-house wall in the evening
walking the Crown to visit the graves
mending a torn apron by the fire
Mirren Quill.calling: Healing is my calling; midwifery is the part of it I love best, because it is the only part that ends in a beginning.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He keeps the book and I keep the bodies; we have never needed to swap.

relations.name: Sabine Quill
relations.label: daughter
relations.note: She has my hands and her father's caution, and a hunger for the Pale I do not understand.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: A kind lad, and kinder than my husband allows; I would not mind him for a son-in-law.

relations.name: Suri Greave
relations.label: patient
relations.note: Expecting her first, and frightened; I will see her through it.

relations.name: Tamsin Hollin
relations.label: friend
relations.note: Suri's sister, and a good glazier; she frets for the baby as much as I do.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: friend
relations.note: He keeps the list of graves; I keep the graves themselves. We have buried a town between us.

relations.name: Otto Brandt
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: He asked me once about the clay under the Crown, and I told him nobody digs there but to bury.

relations.name: Greta Dunmore
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She hears everything at the wash-house wall, and tells me the half of it that matters.

relations.name: Vessa Pontil
relations.label: Glassmaster
relations.note: A hard woman, but she has never once argued with me over a sick worker.

relations.name: Livia Faro
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: A quiet girl at the lamp house; I delivered her, and her parents are gone now.

memories.gist: The fever winter: I nursed the sick and buried nine, and I could not save Iona or Aurel Pontil, nor Matthias Sarro, nor any of them.
I delivered Sabine on a stormy night, and Aldous held the lamp and did not faint.
I laid out Maddy Dunlin and told Rafe her colour would be sea-green, and he wept and agreed.
Suri Greave came to me in the winter and told me she was expecting, and I told her she would be well.
I sat with Anselm Faro when his sister died, and he went out and lit the lamp that same dusk, as he always does.
I told Otto Brandt that the clay under the Crown is not ours to dig, and he did not argue, but he did not agree either.

stances.why: I have buried enough to know that the living are the ones I can still help.
Nobody digs on the Crown except to bury, and I have laid out most of the graves there.
I am forty-nine, and there is no one after me.
I have delivered both kinds of babies and laid out both kinds of dead, and they are the same flesh.
A healer who talks is a healer nobody calls.

Sabine Quill.narrative: I am Benedikt Orme's pupil, and I read the ship-day tablets in the formal script — the only person under thirty who can. Everyone else in Cullet is content with what the island gives them; I want to know what is past the Pale, and I would rather have that answer than any suitor. Ren Sato is kind and I like him, and my father does not approve, and neither, quite, do I. But the tablets are patient, and so am I.
goals: Learn what is past the Pale, more than she wants anyone in Cullet.
Read the hardest tablets in the formal script.
Make up her own mind about Ren Sato, not her father's.
Ask Bram Calloway everything about the Second Thought.
pastimes: reading tablets in the Readers' House
sitting on the Crown bench looking south
walking down to the Fish Steps at dusk
Sabine Quill.calling: The tablets are my calling: to read what the ship days wrote, and to know what lies past the Pale.

relations.name: Aldous Quill
relations.label: father
relations.note: He wants me settled and safe; I want to know what is past the Pale, and we have not found a way to say that to each other.

relations.name: Mirren Quill
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She listens without judging, which is more than my father does.

relations.name: Benedikt Orme
relations.label: teacher
relations.note: He has taught me the script and the patience to read it; I would follow him anywhere he thought worth going.

relations.name: Ren Sato
relations.label: suitor
relations.note: He is kind and patient, and I like him; but I am not sure I want a fisher's life, or any life that stays on this island.

relations.name: Bram Calloway
relations.label: shipwright
relations.note: He is building the only thing that might cross the Combs, and I mean to know everything about it.

relations.name: Alder Fenwick
relations.label: fellow pupil
relations.note: He wants to be a reader, and he is good; I do not mind him following me about.

relations.name: Lark Morrow
relations.label: acquaintance
relations.note: She says she saw a sail beyond the Combs, and everyone laughs; I do not laugh.

relations.name: Roos Achterberg
relations.label: friend
relations.note: She runs the counters game and knows everyone's business; she is good company at the Marver.

relations.name: Hana Sato
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: She gathers kelp with Lark, and she is one of the few who does not laugh at her about the sail; I like her for that, though we have never talked long.

memories.gist: The first time I read a whole ship-day tablet aloud to Benedikt, and he nodded and said nothing, and I knew I had it right.
Ren Sato walked me home from the Fish Steps and my father stood in the doorway and did not ask him in.
Lark Morrow told me she saw a sail beyond the Combs, and her eyes were certain, and I have thought about it since.
I asked Bram Calloway how many trees he needed and he said fourteen, and I understood then that the Hanger was the whole question.
My mother showed me the colour of the glass on Maddy Dunlin's grave and told me why Rafe chose it.
The fever winter: I was thirteen and I helped my mother carry water, and I remember the quiet of the town.

stances.why: The tablets were written by people who knew more than we do, and the Pale is the question they left us.
If anything can cross the Combs, it is the Second Thought, and I mean to know what Bram knows.
My father means well, but he cannot choose my husband or my work for me.
Everything in the Readers' House was written by someone who meant it, and it is our only honest record.
Ren is kind, but kindness will not answer the question I cannot stop asking.
